tests.title: Screen use: decisions, design and home routines

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: Devices counted as screen use include phones, tablets and {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The opening definition includes laptops alongside smartphones and tablets.

questions.prompt: Australian restriction for younger users: access to {{blank}} apps.

evidence.summary: The Australian measure concerns access to social media apps rather than every digital device.

questions.prompt: Goodacre's preferred approach: be more {{blank}} about technology use.

evidence.summary: Goodacre prioritises intentional use instead of simply separating children from technology.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: Why should a designer consider how children learn at different ages?

evidence.summary: The design proposal starts from development and then considers technology as a possible support.

distractors.B: Considering stages implies attention to differences, not ignoring them.
distractors.C: Goodacre speaks about enabling development, not replacing all other learning.

options.label: A
options.text: To explore whether technology can support that development.

options.label: B
options.text: To make the same product suitable for every age without changes.

options.label: C
options.text: To remove all non-digital ways of learning.

questions.prompt: What change in parents' approach is linked to raising the bar?

evidence.summary: The presenter connects the higher bar with more considered parental expectations.

distractors.A: Raising the bar refers to expectations rather than increasing time.
distractors.B: The explanation explicitly gives parents a role in setting expectations.

options.label: A
options.text: A fixed increase in the time allowed on devices.

options.label: B
options.text: Allowing children to set every standard without adult input.

options.label: C
options.text: More careful consideration and higher expectations.

questions.prompt: What is the intended result of a more intentional approach?

evidence.summary: The summary presents technology and development as potentially compatible.

distractors.A: The proposal supports learning and development rather than removing the need to learn.
distractors.C: Development alongside technology is stated, not conditional on complete removal.

options.label: A
options.text: Children no longer need to learn how to manage technology.

options.label: B
options.text: Children can develop while also using technology.

options.label: C
options.text: Children learn only after every device is removed.

groups.heading: Questions 7–8
groups.answerInstruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

questions.prompt: Kennedy describes parents as {{blank}} to understand the relationship between children and technology.

evidence.summary: Kennedy says parents strongly want to understand what is happening with technology and children.

questions.prompt: Parents want realistic actions that they can take in their {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Kennedy locates the desired practical actions in the home.

groups.heading: Questions 9–10
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: What object does Kennedy suggest putting somewhere out of sight? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The concrete intervention is moving the device to a place where it cannot be seen.

questions.prompt: What outcome does Kennedy say the previous arrangement had not prepared the child for? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: Kennedy acknowledges that leaving the screen visible was not setting the child up for success.

sourceReview.method: Official BBC transcript meaning cross-checked with the direct lesson recording; word-timed ASR used only to locate passages.

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: How do the presenters describe their own phone use?

evidence.summary: The opening exchange acknowledges that excessive phone use is not limited to children.

distractors.B: Both explicitly describe excessive use, rather than successful control.
distractors.C: The second presenter agrees with the first about personal overuse.

options.label: A
options.text: Both feel they spend too much time on their phones.

options.label: B
options.text: Both believe their phone use is already well controlled.

options.label: C
options.text: Only one believes that adults can overuse phones.

questions.prompt: How is the UK's position distinguished from Australia's?

evidence.summary: Australia's existing restriction is contrasted with measures under consideration elsewhere.

distractors.A: The UK is described as considering measures, not banning all devices.
distractors.B: The difference between an existing restriction and a proposal is explicit.

options.label: A
options.text: The UK has banned every digital device, while Australia has not acted.

options.label: B
options.text: Both countries have already introduced exactly the same rule.

options.label: C
options.text: The UK is considering similar measures, while Australia has acted.

questions.prompt: Which response best represents Goodacre's position?

evidence.summary: Goodacre favours deliberate use over a blanket removal approach.

distractors.A: Her call for intentional use and higher standards is a call for change now.
distractors.C: She explicitly shifts attention away from simply getting children away from technology.

options.label: A
options.text: Leave technology use unchanged until children are adults.

options.label: B
options.text: Make children's technology use more purposeful.

options.label: C
options.text: Treat complete separation from technology as the main goal.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.answerInstruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

questions.prompt: For Goodacre, a product should be designed with {{blank}} as its first concern.

evidence.summary: The design priority is childhood rather than the appeal of technology itself.

questions.prompt: Designers need to consider how children learn at different {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Goodacre calls attention to developmental differences between stages of childhood.

questions.prompt: The next question is whether technology can {{blank}} that learning and development.

evidence.summary: Technology is presented as a possible means of enabling development already identified as important.

groups.heading: Questions 7–8
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: What subject do parents particularly want to understand in relation to their children? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: Kennedy reports a strong parental wish to understand technology and children.

questions.prompt: What phrase does Kennedy use for manageable adjustments at home? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: Kennedy describes the desired home adjustments as little shifts rather than a complete transformation.

groups.heading: Questions 9–10
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: Environmental cue that creates temptation: a visible {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Kennedy explains that seeing a screen makes wanting to use it a predictable response.

questions.prompt: What the earlier arrangement failed to prepare the child for: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The parent acknowledges a failure to create conditions for success.

tests.title: Standards and small changes: listening for meaning

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.prompt: Which portable computers are included in the explanation of screen time? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The definition includes laptop use as one form of screen time.

questions.prompt: Which type of apps is the Australian restriction aimed at? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The restriction targets a category of apps, namely social media.

questions.prompt: Below what age does the Australian restriction apply? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The age boundary given for the social media restriction is under sixteen.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.answerInstruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

questions.prompt: Quality needed in decisions about children's technology use: being {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Goodacre asks adults to make deliberate decisions about technology use.

questions.prompt: Perspective that should come first in a product: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The product should be considered from the standpoint of childhood first.

questions.prompt: Developmental issue to allow for: children being at different {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Goodacre says the design process must consider different learning and developmental stages.

groups.heading: Questions 7–8
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: What makes an action intentional in the explanation given?

evidence.summary: Intentional behaviour is purposeful and may lead to more careful action.

distractors.A: Intentional use is explicitly distinguished from simply stopping use.
distractors.C: The explanation requires a plan or reason, not an automatic habit.

options.label: A
options.text: It always involves keeping a child away from technology.

options.label: B
options.text: It is guided by a purpose that can make the person act more carefully.

options.label: C
options.text: It happens regularly without any need for a reason.

questions.prompt: What should listeners understand from the demand for a higher bar?

evidence.summary: The phrase refers to standards and expectations rather than a physical position or fixed duration.

distractors.B: The bar is used figuratively for standards, not screen height.
distractors.C: The speaker calls for careful decisions, not a universal benefit from longer sessions.

options.label: A
options.text: Adults should examine their expectations and decisions more carefully.

options.label: B
options.text: Adults should choose physically higher places for all screens.

options.label: C
options.text: Adults should assume that a longer session always means better learning.

groups.heading: Questions 9–10
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: One proposed change is to put the device somewhere it cannot be {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The suggested change removes the device from the child's view.

questions.prompt: Kennedy says leaving the screen visible had not set the child up for {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The example recognises that the arrangement, not merely willpower, affects success.
